title: The engine & drivetrain
dek: A century-old supply chain is on borrowed time as EVs eliminate transmissions and tariffs collapse the margins of engine makers.
lede: The internal combustion engine built America's car industry. But electric motors need no engine. No transmission. No exhaust system. And when millions of vehicles stop needing these parts, an enormous supply chain—774 engine factories, 338 transmission plants, 90,000 transmission workers—wakes up to an existential problem. The electrification is not killing this industry all at once. It's squeezing it from three directions at once: tariffs, shrinking demand, and the slow shift to motors and batteries.
what_changed:
Engine manufacturing seems stable on paper—$43.8 billion in 2026, up from $37.3 billion in 2022. But the growth masks a fundamental shift. The industry is no longer making just gasoline engines. It's awkwardly straddling three fuel types at once: traditional gasoline, hybrids (which need hybrid modules and control systems), and mild-hybrid 48-volt systems. OEMs are keeping gasoline engines alive by turbocharging them, adding variable compression, and bolting on electric assist—buying time rather than investing in the long term. CAFE standards were actually reset in June 2025 to exclude EV credits from compliance, which sounds backwards but tells you everything: the government is giving automakers permission to keep selling cheaper gasoline cars. The real story is in transmission manufacturing, where the decline is brutal. Transmissions went from $54.7 billion in 2022 to $44.6 billion in 2026—a 18% drop. The sector lost 1.5% of establishments and shed 68,000 jobs during 2025 alone. Hybrids temporarily bought some time (hybrid sales jumped 20.5% through mid-2026), because hybrids still need multi-speed transmissions. But battery electric vehicles need nothing—EVs have a single-speed gearbox or go straight electric motor to wheels. Battery electric share collapsed from 9.8% to 5.9% by July 2026 after federal tax credits expired in September 2025, but that was tax policy, not physics. The structural death of transmission demand is baked in.

Tariffs are accelerating the consolidation and killing smaller players. The U.S. imposed 25% tariffs on autos and auto parts in April 2025, then Mexico followed in January 2026 with 25-50% tariffs on non-FTA parts. These tariffs added $2,000 to $4,000 to new vehicle prices and squeezed supplier margins to the breaking point. First Brands (which owned Raybestos, Centric, Cardone, Autolite, and FRAM) filed Chapter 11 in September 2025. TransAxle, a drivetrain remanufacturer with 13 locations in New Jersey, shut down permanently in August 2025 and laid off 209 workers with no bankruptcy filing—just closed the doors. Allison Transmission, trying to survive, spent $2.7 billion to acquire Dana's off-highway drivetrain business in June 2026, consolidating to chase $120 million in annual cost savings. These aren't random bankruptcies. They're signals that the margin model for traditional transmission and engine suppliers is broken. A shop with under $2 million in annual revenue can't absorb tariff costs, labor pressures, and shrinking volumes all at once.

The one bright spot is engine remanufacturing—the business of taking an old engine out of a junkyard, rebuilding it, and reselling it cheaper than a new one. This industry, worth $14.59 billion in 2025, is growing at 4.2% a year through 2033, with hybrid-engine remanufacturing expanding at 16.2% annually. The reason is perverse. New vehicle prices exploded because of tariffs. Interest rates stayed high. Used car supplies dried up. So owners of aging vehicles—the average fleet age jumped from 12.4 years in 2024 to 12.8 years in 2025 and is headed to 13 years by 2026—are choosing to stay with their old cars instead of buying new ones. A $10,000 to $15,000 engine replacement is painful but cheaper than a $35,000 new car at 7% interest. That's keeping the remanufacturing shops alive. But even they are squeezed: 44% of repair parts come from overseas, and tariffs have made sourcing engine cores 15-25% more expensive year-on-year. Shops need certification for hybrid and diesel work—labor costs rise. Metals stay expensive. Smaller remanufacturers with low margins (5-7%) can't hold on and are being swallowed by larger regional consolidators.

Transmission Market Pressure: Hybrid sales jumped 20.5% through mid-2026, but BEV market share fell to 5.9% by July 2026 after EV tax credit expiration September 2025; light vehicle sales hit 16.3 million annualized in July 2026, down 1.4% YoY.

Engine Remanufacturing Revival: $14.59 billion market in 2025, growing 4.2% CAGR through 2033; hybrid-engine remanufacturing at 16.2% CAGR; average US vehicle fleet age hit 12.8 years in May 2025 (up from 12.6 years in 2024), reaching 13 years by 2026.
win: Consolidators win. Denso, Bosch, and Continental are doubling down on EV electronics and thermal systems, positioning themselves as powertrain integrators rather than pure engine makers. Allison Transmission won by acquiring Dana's drivetrain assets for $2.7 billion and chasing $120 million in annual synergies. Remanufacturing shops in regional clusters survive and grow by servicing older fleets—that market is expanding 4.2% a year. And OEMs that can stretch gasoline engine life through turbocharging and 48-volt mild-hybrid systems buy time before committing fully to EV-only lineups. The winners are those big enough to pivot, not those tied to a single fuel type.
lose: Small and mid-sized suppliers lose. First Brands filed Chapter 11 in September 2025. TransAxle shut down all 13 locations in August 2025 with no bankruptcy—just done. Transmission workers lose: the sector shed 68,000 jobs in 2025 alone. Shops with under $2 million in annual revenue can't absorb tariff costs and are being consolidated. Gas station owners and fuel distributors lose as EV adoption eventually replaces pump demand. New-vehicle dealers lose margin as competition from used cars (kept alive by cheap engine remanufacturing) intensifies. And the traditional transmission maker—a company built on the skill of designing five-speed automatics—has no real future. That skill is obsolete in an electric-motor world.
worry: The biggest risk is that tariffs and geopolitical tensions spiral further, collapsing vehicle demand before the supply chain can adapt. Light vehicle sales are already weakening (16.3 million annualized in July 2026, down 1.4% YoY). If tariffs double, or if U.S.-China tensions push localization further, smaller suppliers may fail en masse before they can retool for EV components. The industry is caught between dying gasoline platforms and expensive EV platforms—there's no third option. A recession that cuts new-vehicle sales even 5% more could trigger a cascade of bankruptcies across transmission plants, engine remanufacturers, and parts suppliers. Consolidation is efficient but also fragile: it concentrates risk into a few large players (Allison, Denso, Bosch) and leaves regional suppliers and workers with nowhere to go.
one_sentence: Engines and transmissions are not disappearing overnight—hybrids and tariffs are keeping them alive—but the supply chain is shrinking, consolidating, and losing 68,000 jobs a year as the mathematics of electric vehicles crush the demand for parts that motors simply don't need.

title: Exhaust, Fuel & the Gas Station
dek: The engine's slow death leaves behind a stranded infrastructure of catalytic converters, gas stations, and fuel retail fighting to survive.
lede: Gas stations still line every highway and city corner in America—147,000 of them across the country in 2026. But the fundamental business is breaking. Fuel margins hover at just 1–2% per gallon, fuel volumes dropped 5.4% in 2025, and electric vehicles are eating into the core reason these stations exist. Meanwhile, the catalytic converter—the device that treated exhaust from tens of millions of cars—is becoming obsolete as EVs eliminate the need for it entirely.
what_changed:
For a century, the gas station was the backbone of automotive retail. You bought fuel. That's it. But by 2025–2026, that model is cracking. Gas prices fell 5.9% in 2025 to $3.11 per gallon, and fuel volume plummeted from $501.9 billion in 2024 to $476.3 billion in 2025—a 5.4% drop in a single year. Electric vehicles hit 4.5 million registered units in 2025, growing 26.7% year-over-year, and though the federal tax credit expired in September 2025 (causing new EV sales to crater from 10.5% of the market to just 5.8%), the long trend is unmistakable. Gas stations can no longer survive on fuel alone.

The industry's response has been to abandon fuel as the profit center and rebuild around convenience merchandise and prepared food. In 2026, convenience stores with gas pumps—a $678.9 billion industry—squeeze roughly 40 cents profit per gallon on fuel while chasing margin in hot dogs, coffee, and grab-and-go meals. Inside sales account for 28.5% of revenue now, and foodservice and merchandise hit $341.2 billion in 2025. But even that isn't enough to offset the squeeze: operating expenses rose faster than sales, shrinking per-transaction margins by 7 cents in 2025. Labor costs run $300,000–$500,000 per store annually and are climbing 3.3% each year, while tariffs (25% on Mexican auto parts since January 2025, with Mexico firing back with 5–50% retaliatory tariffs in January 2026) are making everything from coffee makers to point-of-sale systems more expensive. Major chains are retreating: Shell divested 500 company-owned retail sites per year in 2024–2025 to focus on refining. The result is consolidation—Alimentation Couche-Tard closed a $1.57 billion acquisition of GetGo Cafe + Market in June 2025 and snapped up Hutch's the same month, while total gas station count contracted 1.4% annually since 2021.

Catalytic converters—the $9.87 billion US manufacturing sector that treats exhaust emissions—face a steeper cliff. The global market is forecast to contract at -5.7% CAGR through 2034, shrinking from $18.1 billion to $12.3 billion, because electric cars simply don't produce exhaust. The US market is technically still growing at 3.92% CAGR through 2035, but that's a mirage: it's sustained by an aging vehicle fleet (average age over 12 years) forcing emissions upgrades and by a temporary surge in aftermarket theft and replacement. In late 2025, platinum, palladium, and rhodium staged a substantial recovery on South African supply deficits, triggering a catalytic converter theft explosion—137,000+ units stolen in 2025 compared to roughly 14,000 in 2024. That's a ninefold spike, driven purely by precious-metal prices and the scrap value of old converters. But it's a death rattle, not a sign of health. Repair shops and OEM suppliers are hedging by pouring R&D into hybrid-vehicle catalysts and selective catalytic reduction technology. Meanwhile, tariff shocks are killing already-thin margins—manufacturers run 5–6% net margins in 2025–2026, and tariffs are narrowing them further, forcing smaller players out and consolidating the sector around Tenneco, Johnson Matthey, Faurecia, Umicore, BASF Catalysts, and a shrinking roster of others.

What electrification made scarce: profitable retail fuel business and the entire exhaust-treatment supply chain. What it made cheap: gasoline, which dropped 5.9% in 2025 as demand flattened, and convenience stations, as weaker operators shut down and major brands divest. What it made risky: being a stand-alone gas station operator or a mid-tier catalytic converter supplier dependent on aging vehicles. What it made newly valuable: the ability to lock customers into prepared food and inside merchandise (Costco and Walmart are already winning the fuel price war by undercutting independent stations by 20–35 cents per gallon), automation and labor efficiency in convenience retail, and recycling of precious metals from old converters.

Non-traditional fuel retailers like Costco and Walmart win by using fuel as a loss leader to drive traffic for higher-margin grocery and goods. In catalytic converter manufacturing, survivors are those investing in hybrid catalysts and advanced emissions tech (Johnson Matthey, Umicore expanding R&D in 2025–2026) or those with scale to absorb tariff shocks and consolidate around premium, high-tech variants.
lose: Stand-alone gas station operators and mid-tier convenience store chains are squeezed by razor-thin margins (1–2% on fuel, eroding per-transaction margins inside stores) and rising labor costs ($300K–$500K per store annually, climbing 3.3% each year). Smaller catalytic converter suppliers face margin compression from tariffs and must compete against consolidated giants—the sector counted 150–200 establishments but faces ongoing M&A pressure. SQRL Service Stations, a significant operator, liquidated in Chapter 7 bankruptcy in 2024 after filing Chapter 11 with a $1.2 billion debt burden, signaling the financial stress of traditional gas station economics.
worry: The temporary reprieve from EV tax credit expiration (new EV sales crashed to 5.8% in Q4 2025) masks the underlying destruction: 4.5 million registered EVs in 2025, growing 26.7% year-over-year, will eventually represent 8% of used-car returns by 2026, meaning fuel demand will continue its structural decline. Gas station operators have shifted to inside merchandise and prepared food, but that business is hitting margin limits (per-transaction margins shrank 7 cents in 2025), and it attracts intense price competition from Costco and Walmart. Catalytic converter manufacturers are facing a -5.7% global CAGR contraction, and tariff shocks will accelerate consolidation and supply-chain fragmentation. The entire ecosystem—gas stations, convenience stores, fuel distribution, and emissions treatment—built for a century of internal-combustion dominance, is slowly becoming stranded.
one_sentence: As electric vehicles grow inexorably and fuel demand shrinks, gas stations and catalytic converter makers are trapped between structural decline, razor-thin margins, rising costs, and tariff shocks, forcing consolidation and a desperate pivot to convenience merchandise that can't fully replace the vanishing fuel business.

title: The Repair Aftermarket
dek: Oil changes are dying, transmission shops have fewer customers, and the century-old parts economy is shrinking.
one_sentence: The electric car needs far less maintenance—no oil changes, simpler drivetrains, regenerative brakes—and the $77 billion US auto parts retail industry and the body shops that depend on routine repairs are slowing to a crawl while tariffs, consolidation, and a collapsing technician pipeline hollow out the independents.
lede: The electric car needs far less servicing. No oil changes. No spark plugs. Regenerative braking means brake pads last longer. This simple fact is hollowing out an industry that turned wrenches for one hundred years. The repair shops, parts stores, and remanufacturers built on the gasoline engine are watching their core business dry up, even as the cars themselves get older.
what_changed:
Electric vehicles structurally need fewer repairs and fewer parts than gas cars, and this is now showing up in the numbers. The US auto parts retail market—$77.1 billion in 2026—is growing at only 1.6% annually, a grinding slowdown, because every Tesla or Chevy Bolt that replaces a gas car is a car that no longer needs an oil change every 3,000 miles, no longer needs spark plugs, no longer needs transmission fluid topped up, and no longer burns through brake pads the same way. The average vehicle on the road is now 12.8 years old (a record as of 2025), which should mean more repairs—but electrification cancels that benefit. Meanwhile, e-commerce—Amazon alone did $13.7 billion in auto parts in 2026—has pulled the price-sensitive DIY buyer straight online, bypassing the corner parts store. The result is a retail network designed for peak volume that is slowly starving.

The collision repair shops—$67.7 billion industry in 2026, growing at only 0.6% annually—face a parallel squeeze. Repairable collision claims dropped over 10% in 2025, signaling that cars themselves are safer (ADAS systems preventing crashes before they happen). But when a repair does arrive, it is now far more complicated and expensive. Sensor calibration for advanced driver assist systems runs $300 to $800 per repair and adds 37.6% to the total bill; these recalibrations now show up in one-third of all direct repair program estimates. The shops that can afford the training and equipment for ADAS work are consolidating: Boyd Group bought Joe Hudson's (258 locations, $1.3 billion) in January 2026; Gerber expanded by 311 shops in 2025; Caliber filed for a public offering in July 2025 and has grown to 1,863 locations. The 68.7% of shops that remain independent—105,000 total—cannot compete. The industry needs 110,000 new technicians by 2026 but attracts almost none; median wage is $47,670, and shop owners report being unable to fill entry-level slots. Insurance reimbursement rates lag the rising cost and complexity of work, and deductibles have climbed—over one in four drivers now carry $1,000+ deductibles—so many skip claims entirely rather than pay out of pocket. The shops are trapped between falling volume and rising technical demand.

The remanufacturing sector—which takes used parts apart, restores them, and sells them for 50% less than new—is experiencing a harder blow. The US remanufactured parts market is estimated at $5.2 billion (2021 baseline) and projects to $74 billion globally by 2026, but that growth masks a fundamental transition. For decades, remanufacturing meant taking old engines, transmissions, alternators, and starters apart, restoring them, and selling them cheap to budget-conscious repair shops and fleet operators. Those parts are becoming obsolete. EV powertrains—high-voltage batteries, electric motors, controllers—require entirely different skills and certification. The remanufactured battery and motor segment is growing at 21.8% annually and projected to hit $12.8 billion by 2034, but it is a small base starting from $2.1 billion in 2025. Worse, the industry was hit by a shock in September 2025 when First Brands Group (parent of Cardone, the largest North American remanufacturer) filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy with $9.3 billion in obligations, allegedly tied to a $2.3 billion factoring fraud. Over 1,200 jobs were cut across Ohio and other facilities. The 25% tariff on imported auto parts (April 2025) further compressed margins—import volumes fell 10% year-over-year, which helped North American suppliers gain market share from 41% to 44%, but only for those with scale and domestic supply chains. Smaller remanufacturers, already displaced by the battery transition, were ground between Cardone's collapse and tariff costs.

What made this scarce: routine maintenance work. What made this cheap: remanufactured gasoline-engine components. What made this risky: being a mid-sized parts retailer or remanufacturer bet on internal combustion. What became newly valuable: battery remanufacturing, ADAS repair expertise, and the scale to absorb tariff shocks and train technicians for software-defined car systems.

The large collision repair consolidators—Boyd, Gerber, Caliber—are also winning: they can afford ADAS equipment, technician training pipelines, and absorb insurance reimbursement lags. Battery remanufacturers and circular-economy players backed by OEM commitments and environmental regulation are winning because they are riding a 21.8% annual growth tailwind into a segment with no legacy incumbent dominance.
lose: Independent auto parts retailers are being squeezed out by e-commerce and tariffs; smaller collision repair shops (68.7% of 105,000 shops are still independent) cannot afford ADAS training and equipment, cannot compete on price or volume, and face insurance reimbursement rates that lag rising technical complexity. The entire skilled trades pipeline is collapsing: the industry needs 110,000 new technicians by 2026 but median wage is $47,670, average technician age is 41, women comprise only 3% of the workforce, and 95% of shop owners cannot fill entry-level slots. Mid-sized remanufacturers hit by the Cardone bankruptcy and tariff volatility (import volumes fell 10% in 2025) are being liquified or acquired at fire-sale prices.
worry: The labor crisis is the single biggest risk. The repair industry needs 110,000 new technicians by 2026 but attracts almost none. Average age is 41, gender diversity is near zero, and wages—$47,670 median—are not competitive against software engineering, skilled trades in renewables, or the skilled manufacturing jobs now returning to the US due to reshoring incentives. If the talent pipeline fails, repair shops will close or turn customers away, collision estimates will take months instead of weeks, used-car values will compress (because fleet managers worry about repair availability), and the entire used-vehicle aftermarket will seize. The second risk is tariff volatility: the 25% tariff on parts (April 2025) dropped to 30% in a 90-day truce (May 2025), and this whipsaws inventory planning, squeezes margins further, and accelerates bankruptcies among smaller players. A return to 25% would be devastating.

title: The battery is the new engine
dek: The car's power source went from commodity fuel to specialized hardware—and created an entirely new supply chain nobody quite knows how to run yet.
lede: For a hundred years, the engine was the car. You swapped oil, rebuilt transmissions, and scrapped cars for a few hundred bucks. That machine is over. Now the battery is what costs $10,000 to $15,000, determines range and power, and has to be made, recycled, and managed like a critical material. The whole industry is racing to build capacity for a wave of EVs that won't actually arrive for years—and in the meantime, billions of dollars are sitting in half-empty factories.
what_changed:
US battery manufacturing exploded on paper. From 2021 to 2026, the industry grew from $9.7 billion to $61.1 billion—a 38.5% compound annual growth rate, driven by the Inflation Reduction Act and automaker bets. The Feds and companies poured $27+ billion into new capacity, expecting EVs to fill every factory. Capacity jumped from 90 GWh in 2022 to over 160 GWh by 2026. It should have been a triumph. But reality hit. EV sales growth stalled. Panasonic delayed its Kansas gigafactory ramp in July 2025, pushing back 30 GWh of capacity. GM halted production at two Ultium plants in Ohio and Tennessee in late 2025, pausing through mid-2026 while the company figured out what to actually make. The problem was simple: the cars weren't coming fast enough. Factories built for 2023 demand were running 30-40% full by 2025. Volume dropped. Margins compressed. The battery industry, which had invested in scale, was drowning in it.

So manufacturers pivoted hard. GM and LG retooled their Spring Hill, Tennessee plant to make lithium iron phosphate batteries for grid storage instead of cars—a $70 million retool that started in March 2026. LG Energy Solution began targeting 60+ GWh of LFP storage capacity globally. US LFP cell production grew 30% year-over-year to 57.6 GWh in 2025. It was the only growth lever left. The trouble is that energy storage margins are thinner than EV batteries, and grid storage itself is already approaching oversupply in the US by 2026. Manufacturers are chasing a market that's also filling up.

Meanwhile, battery recycling—supposed to be the circular-economy hero—is broken. The recycling market reached $6.76 billion in 2025 but is growing at only 9.81% CAGR through 2035 while lithium-ion recycling itself sprints at 22.24% CAGR. That sounds good until you look at the actual numbers. Recycling capacity in the US hit 144,000 tons in 2024 and is racing to 300,000 tons by 2026. But the feedstock won't arrive. The EV recycling wave won't hit 1.3 million units annually until 2030 at earliest. Plants are running 25-30% full. The real killer is chemistry. NMC and NCM batteries (nickel-heavy, older designs) yield about $1,700 per pack in recovered value before operating costs. LFP batteries—which are now rising fast in EVs because they're cheaper and safer—often have negative recovery value. Recyclers lose money on them. In April 2026, Ascend Elements filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy after the DOE canceled $480 million in grants due to slipping timelines. Redwood Materials, which raised $425 million in a January 2026 funding round, cut 10% of its workforce (135 jobs) in early 2026 due to Chinese battery price pressure. The second-life battery market—storing EV packs in grids for 5-10 years instead of shredding them immediately—is filling the void, with 120 GWh of EV packs worldwide reaching end-of-vehicle life in 2026 at 70-80% capacity. But that delays economics, not fixes them.

The core shift is this: the battery went from a fungible commodity (oil) to a specialty asset (engineered hardware) that has to be sourced, managed, and recovered like a natural resource. That made mining, refining, and recycling into bottlenecks. Clarios announced a $6 billion ten-year investment plan in 2026, allocating $1.9 billion for critical minerals processing and $2.5 billion for advanced battery expansion. The industry is betting that it can control its own supply chain. But it's also locked into a bet that didn't pay off fast enough.

title: The Car Becomes a Computer
dek: Software and chips now define the car, not mechanics — and the supply chain is tearing itself apart.
lede: The electric car runs on software. Battery management, autonomous-driving sensors, in-cabin AI, over-the-air updates — none of that exists in a car with a combustion engine. The moment automakers go EV, the whole bill of materials flips. Electronics and semiconductors go from a small cost in the car's total to the bulk of it. But the US supply chain for making those boards and chips is cracking under the weight of change.
what_changed: US automobile electronics manufacturing brought in $29.6 billion in revenue in 2025, down 3 percent from 2022 — even as automakers were ordering more EV-grade systems than ever. The margin is squeezed to 4.7 percent, and employment has stalled at around 58,000 to 60,000 workers. What's happening is a bifurcation: large suppliers like Lear and Visteon are surviving by automating and consolidating around EV capabilities. Lear hit $6.0 billion in Q4 2025 revenue, up 5 percent year-over-year, and Visteon guided to $3.625 billion to $3.825 billion for 2026. But smaller Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers are filing for bankruptcy at record rates. In 2025 alone, supplier bankruptcies exceeded any year in the past decade. First Brands Group, which carried $6 billion in debt, filed for Chapter 11 in May 2025. Accuride and Fisker collapsed in 2024 and 2025. The tariff wall made it worse. In January 2026, the US imposed a 25 percent tariff on advanced semiconductor components and threatened broader measures. But automakers had locked suppliers into fixed-fee contracts years ago. Companies couldn't renegotiate easily, so the tariff cost fell on them. They had to absorb the hit or go under. Meanwhile, Mexico is eating their lunch. In 2024, automotive investment in Mexico reached $8 billion, and Mexico was constructing 2,274 hectares of new manufacturing space by end-2025. Foxconn built a $900 million AI-server campus there. ASE put down a $200 million advanced-packaging line. Nearshoring is cheaper and faces no tariffs. The result: domestic volume is shrinking even as the dollar value of each car's electronics content rises. The printed-circuit-board industry — the substrate everything sits on — is in similar distress. Circuit board and component manufacturing brought in $61.3 billion in 2026, up only 1 percent over five years and actually declining 0.5 percent in 2026 alone. Margins are flat at around 6 percent, under pressure from input costs and price wars. But the bifurcation here is even starker. AI servers and 5G infrastructure are driving explosive demand for high-complexity, high-density boards. Layer counts have jumped from 16 to 20 layers up to 28 to 36 layers. AI servers went from 15 percent of PCB demand in 2025 to over 25 percent in 2026. The players with capital are investing. TTM Technologies opened a new Ultra-HDI (ultra-high-density interconnect) facility in Syracuse, New York in June 2026, designed for aerospace and defense. Jabil announced a $500 million multi-year expansion for US cloud computing and AI data-center hardware, starting mid-2026. Ventec International is building a $17 million facility in Thailand to serve the US and Asia. TTM acquired a 750,000-square-foot facility in Eau Claire, Wisconsin for advanced PCB production targeting data-center networking. But mid-tier and small players are getting squeezed out. TTM itself closed plants in Anaheim and Santa Clara in 2024 and 2025. Camston Wrather liquidated. Import tariffs of 25 to 35 percent on Chinese PCBs made it expensive to buy overseas, but US domestic capacity is so bottlenecked that new customers face long waits just for quotes. Many shops refuse new orders. This created a pricing window for whoever can expand — but expansion requires capital that smaller shops don't have. The bifurcation has created a three-way chasm: large, well-capitalized suppliers that can automate and go after aerospace, AI, and next-gen EV platforms; nearshore or overseas manufacturers in Mexico, Thailand, and China competing on cost; and everyone else, shrinking.

title: Electrification's hunger for copper
dek: EVs need 2.9 times more copper than gas engines, and a supply crunch is already here.
one_sentence: The switch to electric cars is pulling copper from the ground faster than mines can dig, and the whole mining and metals industry is racing to catch up.
lede: Electric vehicles need nearly three times as much copper as gas cars. Add in power grids upgrading for renewable energy, and copper suddenly went from a commodity that was plentiful to one that is scarce. Prices have doubled since 2023, and the shortage is real—500,000 tonnes missing from the global market in 2026.
what_changed:
When you swap an internal combustion engine for batteries and a motor, you're swapping steel and iron for copper wiring, battery terminals, and grid infrastructure. An EV needs 2.9 times the copper of a gas car just for the drivetrain, and then the power grid that charges those cars needs even more—substations, transmission lines, transformers, all copper-hungry. By May 2026, copper futures hit an all-time high of $6.58 per pound, capping a 40.86 percent gain over the prior twelve months. The price surge came from exactly one place: EVs and renewable energy went from "the future" to "happening right now," and the mines that supply the world couldn't dig fast enough. Global copper demand hit 27.2 million tonnes in 2025, but supply fell short by 500,000 tonnes forecast for 2026. That is the shortfall that made copper expensive and scrambled the entire value chain.

The US copper mining sector, which pulled in $13.8 billion in 2026, faces a crisis of timing. American ore grades are declining—meaning each tonne of rock yields less copper—and major expansion projects like Resolution Copper (a joint venture with Rio Tinto and BHP) won't produce until the mid-2030s. The same permitting delays that hamstring every big mine in the US mean that even though copper prices are at record highs, new supply cannot flood the market fast enough to erase the shortage. Instead, the US has turned to tariffs. In August 2025, the Trump administration slapped a 50 percent Section 232 tariff on semi-refined copper imports, and by 2027, a 15 to 30 percent broad copper tariff looms. The tariffs were designed to protect domestic smelting and refining, but they also locked in higher prices for anyone downstream who needs copper—the manufacturers and construction companies that actually build with it.

Copper rolling and drawing plants—the factories that turn raw copper cathode into wires, tubes, and sheets—expanded to near full capacity in 2025 and 2026 to feed the surge. The market size jumped from $31.8 billion in 2022 to $41.3 billion in 2026, a 30 percent surge in four years. Plants that process copper are running twenty-four-seven and still cannot keep pace. Southwire, the largest wire maker in the US, acquired United Copper Industries in February 2026 specifically to expand capacity for building wire and EV battery harnesses. But here is the trap: the 50 percent tariff on imported semi-finished copper eliminated foreign competition and pushed prices to $13,842 per tonne in January 2026. Smaller processors got squeezed hard. They cannot raise prices fast enough to pass on the tariff costs to customers, working capital strains, and delivery times stretch. The big players weather it; the mid-market gets caught in between.

Aluminum tells a parallel story but with a twist. EV makers need aluminum for battery enclosures and body panels to offset the weight of the battery pack, and aluminum prices surged 25 percent year-over-year by August 2026 to $3,273 per tonne. But the US primary smelting sector—just four smelters making 683,500 tonnes per year—cannot expand because electricity costs have hit $115 or more per megawatt-hour. Data centers and AI chip makers are outbidding aluminum smelters for renewable power. The result: 85 percent of US-made aluminum is now recycled, up from just 20 to 30 percent in the 1980s. Recycled aluminum is cheaper and cleaner, and it scales fast. Novelis and Century Aluminum raced to restart or open capacity in 2025 and 2026, but primary smelting remains half-idled. The electrification is pulling EVs forward, but it is also bidding away the electricity that smelters need. That creates a strange constraint: materials abundance (recycled metal) collides with electricity scarcity.

If the price stays elevated, EV makers will redouble efforts to substitute aluminum or other materials, but that pivot takes time and redesign. title: Financing the switch
dek: When the car goes electric, the money stops flowing the old way.
lede: For a century, car finance worked on a simple logic: you borrow, you drive, the car holds value. But EV residual values just collapsed. A three-year-old EV that was worth 90% of its purchase price in 2022 is worth 40% today. That breaks the math for every lease, every captive lender, every used-car dealer. Now the whole auto-finance system is seizing up.
what_changed:
The US auto-finance market entered 2026 in crisis. Market size was $173.8 billion in 2026, declining 2% from 2025 as affordability collapsed and credit deteriorated. Monthly payments for new cars now run $750 and up — versus $600-650 in 2022 — because of tariffs (vehicles up $3,000-$10,000), higher interest rates (6.39% average in Q1 2026 versus historic lows), and lending stretching to 84-96 month terms just to keep payments manageable. New-vehicle registrations fell 6% year-over-year despite used-car inventory climbing 5%, signaling buyers are stepping back entirely. Subprime delinquencies hit 6.6% in January 2025, the highest in 31 years, and by Q1 2026, 90+ day delinquencies reached 5.6% — all-time record — pushing repossession toward 3 million vehicles in 2025, matching the Great Recession. The subprime sector is imploding: Tricolor Holdings, one of the largest used-car dealers and subprime lenders, liquidated in October 2025 amid fraud allegations and massive delinquencies. Margins are compressing hard, down to 27-28% from historical 30%+, as lenders build reserves and absorb credit losses.

But the real knife is EV residual value. Late 2025 data shows a $10+ billion loss cascade: captive lenders like Ford Credit and GM Financial locked into EV lease portfolios backed by residual-value estimates that were 50-60 percentage points too high. An off-lease vehicle surge of 25.7% is coming in 2026, flooding wholesale markets and pushing 3-year-old cars down to an average of $31,548. Lessees stopped signing EV leases because nobody knows what that car will be worth in 36 months — the cornerstone assumption of lease economics is shattered. Fleet car leasing, a $10.6 billion US market growing at 3.7% annually, is also choking: tariff shocks (US weighted-average rates hit 20% in mid-2025, with 25% on Mexican and Canadian vehicles) forced operators to choose between eating $5,000-$8,900 per vehicle or jacking prices when corporate customers were already price-sensitive. Operators who specialize in EV fleet conversions are particularly exposed because the residual-value cliff means a $45,000 three-year EV lease deal can become deeply underwater before the lease matures.

Prime borrowers — those with 720+ credit scores — are weathering it because they have cushion. Prime originations stayed at $99.4 billion in Q1 2026. Top-tier lenders like Ally are even seeing lease volumes up 28.6% year-over-year, capturing a bigger slice of a shrinking pie. But subprime, where buy-here-pay-here dealers and credit-focused lenders operate, is shattered. Subprime originations are down despite total volume gains, and the largest used-car specialists are either filing for bankruptcy or retreating to credit-card and fintech pivots — Atlanticus Holdings acquired Mercury Financial in September 2025 to diversify away from auto. The three-way squeeze — unaffordable payments, record delinquencies, and EV depreciation uncertainty — is wiping out dealers and lenders who can't weather repricing, refinancing, or taking losses on lease returns.

title: The electrification
dek: Value drains from the engine and the pump to the battery, the chip, and the mine.
lede: Electric cars don't just swap an engine for a battery. They tear up the century-old machine that made gasoline cars cheap and simple. Engines, transmissions, gas stations, and all the parts that went into them built entire industries. Batteries, semiconductors, copper, and software are building different ones. The shift is real but lumpy—some pieces are dying, others are being stretched and contorted to survive.
what_changed:
US battery manufacturing grew from $9.7 billion in 2021 to $61.1 billion in 2026—a 38.5% annual growth rate powered by $27+ billion in federal subsidies and automaker investment. Capacity tripled in five years, from 90 GWh in 2022 to over 160 GWh by 2026. But here's the problem: demand stopped growing. EV sales growth has slowed sharply in the US. Panasonic delayed its Kansas battery plant ramp in July 2025 by 30 GWh because EV demand wasn't there. General Motors shut down Ultium production at two plants through mid-2026. The industry built warehouses for cars nobody's yet buying at these prices. Margins got crushed—manufacturers pivoted frantically to energy storage, a thinner-margin business. By 2026, grid energy storage is already approaching oversupply despite the build-out, which means even the fallback plan is weakening.

What made copper and nickel valuable was the opposite problem: supply can't catch up. An EV uses 2.9 times more copper than a gas car. Renewable energy infrastructure needs even more. Copper prices doubled from 2023 lows to $6.58 per pound in May 2026—an all-time high—because mines can't scale fast enough. A 500,000-tonne supply shortfall is forecast for 2026 alone. Arizona's mines are hitting declining ore grades. Major expansion projects like Resolution Copper won't start producing until the mid-2030s. Lundin Mining sold its Eagle nickel mine to Talon Metals in December 2025, marking a retreat from US mining by a large player because smaller, remote operations can't stay profitable at those scales. Copper was made scarce and valuable by a force nobody controlled—EV adoption just needed to happen a little, everywhere at once.

Gas stations were made irrelevant by a temporary reprieve. The federal EV tax credit expired on September 30, 2025, and EV sales crashed from 10.5% share in Q3 2025 to 5.8% by Q4 2025 and into 2026. Suddenly, fuel demand stopped collapsing. The gas station industry, which had been contracting—147,000 total stations in 2026, down 1.4% annually since 2021—got a breathing room that might not last. But the business itself became structurally worse. Fuel margins are razor-thin: 1-2% per gallon. Convenience stores and prepared food now account for 28.5% of in-store sales; that's where operators chase profit. Shell exited 500 gas stations per year in 2024-2025 to focus on upstream refining. Costco and Walmart undercut gas prices by 20-35 cents per gallon in their pockets, starting price wars that destroy margins for independent operators. Crude is forecast to fall to $52 per barrel in 2026, keeping retail prices low and crushing what little margin was left.

Gasoline engines themselves didn't die; they mutated. Gasoline engine parts manufacturing stayed near flat—$43.8 billion in 2026 versus $37.3 billion in 2022, a meager 1.5% CAGR. OEMs stretched the life of gasoline platforms instead of replacing them. Turbocharging, variable compression, and 48-volt mild-hybrid systems became the way to eke out more miles per gallon and comply with a weakened CAFE standard (which in June 2025 stopped allowing EV credits to count toward compliance). Tariffs—US 25% on auto parts effective April 2025, Mexico 25-50% on non-FTA parts starting January 2026—forced suppliers into nearshoring and consolidation. Smaller players like First Brands filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2025. Denso, Bosch, and Continental doubled down on EV electronics and thermal systems instead of engines. Engines became a support system for hybrid modules and software. That's the shift: the platform is no longer the engine, and the supplier landscape is being squeezed down to those who can manage complexity in powertrains, not just blocks and bolts.

Auto engines: $43.8 billion market in 2026 (1.5% CAGR since 2021) as OEMs pivot to 48-volt mild-hybrid and turbo platforms; CAFE rules reset June 2025 to exclude EV credits
EV tax credit expiration: Federal credit ended September 30, 2025, causing EV market share to plunge from 10.5% (Q3 2025) to 5.8% (Q4 2025 onward), temporarily halting fuel demand destruction
win: Battery and chip makers, copper miners, and EV OEMs win—but unevenly. Battery makers have the scale (50,000+ employees by 2026) and federal protection to survive the current contraction; the pivots to energy storage and LFP chemistry are showing real volumes (57.6 GWh of US LFP cell production in 2025, up 30% year-over-year). Copper and nickel mining win because the demand is real, even if permitting is broken—Talon Metals bought Eagle for $84 million and plans aggressive exploration because US nickel is half the nation's supply. Semiconductor and software suppliers (Denso, Bosch, Continental) are rewarded for complexity; they're the integrators now, not the engine makers. Costco and Walmart win at gas stations—they use fuel as a loss leader to drive store traffic and compensation the margin loss with prepared food and convenience margins of 7-8%. Tesla and Chinese EV makers win if adoption recovers because they've burned through years of losses to prove the platform works; the capital-intensive first-mover is finally becoming an asset again.
lose: Gasoline engine suppliers and independent gas station operators get squeezed hardest. Engine parts makers lost pricing power—flat 1.5% growth since 2021—and face tariff shocks (25% on US auto parts effective April 2025, 25-50% on Mexican non-FTA parts starting January 2026) that force smaller suppliers like First Brands into bankruptcy (Chapter 11, September 2025). Independent gas stations have nowhere to hide. Fuel margins are 1-2%; convenience margins are 7-8%; but you can't run a station on just snacks. Major chains like Shell are exiting retail (500 sites per year in 2024-2025) and focusing on profitable refining upstream. Crude is forecast to fall to $52 per barrel in 2026, keeping prices low and crushing what remains. Oil and refining companies that relied on retail networks lose retail presence and are forced to become upstream-only players—profitable but smaller in scope. Lundin Mining's exit from US nickel signals that traditional mining companies can't compete in the smaller, remote, capital-intensive US operations anymore; consolidation is squeezing out mid-tier players.
worry: The biggest risk is that demand never catches up to the battery and copper build-out, and the whole system breaks under its own weight. Battery manufacturers built 160 GWh of US capacity on the bet that EV adoption would keep climbing. It didn't. GM paused Ultium production. Panasonic delayed its Kansas ramp by 30 GWh. Energy storage was supposed to be the fallback, but by 2026 grid storage is already approaching oversupply. If that's true, then the $27 billion in subsidies and automaker investment was spent on idle capacity. Copper is the reverse problem: mines can't scale, permitting is broken, and Resolution Copper won't produce until the mid-2030s. If EVs finally do take off—or if renewable buildout accelerates—then the supply shortage becomes a genuine bottleneck, and copper stays expensive, which makes EVs stay expensive, which keeps adoption slow. Either way, something breaks: either overcapacity and wasted capital (batteries), or undersupply and stalled growth (copper). The gap between supply and demand was supposed to close; instead it's widening in both directions at once.
one_sentence: The electrification made batteries expensive to build and copper expensive to find, while engines and gas stations became structurally unprofitable, squeezing suppliers and operators caught in between the old machine and the new one.

title: Insuring the EV
dek: Higher repair costs and battery risk reprice auto insurance and warranties.
one_sentence: The electric car breaks the insurance math that has worked for a century—repair costs are rising faster than premiums, batteries fail in ways engines never did, and an already-broken industry is forced to rebuild its pricing model on data that barely exists.
lede: The electric car breaks the math that auto insurers have relied on for a century. Repair costs are rising faster than premiums can follow, batteries fail in ways gasoline engines never did, and the industry—already trapped in back-to-back years of massive losses—is being forced to rebuild its entire pricing model on the fly.
what_changed:
The commercial auto insurance market lost 4.9 billion USD in 2024 alone, with liability claims reaching 6.4 billion USD—the worst single year on record. For 13 consecutive years, the industry has paid out more in claims than it collected in premiums, a death spiral that only works because investment income masks the rot underneath. The numbers kept getting worse: in 2024, corporate defendants lost 135 nuclear verdict cases totaling 31.3 billion USD in awards, a 52% jump from the year before. The median nuclear verdict hit 51 million USD. The industry raised rates 9-15% annually just to slow the bleeding, but it wasn't enough. By 2025-2026, the damage had accumulated so badly that some carriers started exiting markets entirely or redesigning their entire risk model.

Enter the EV. Repair costs for electric vehicles run 20-40% higher than gas cars, and the industry has almost no historical data on battery replacement costs, degradation curves, or what happens when a battery dies at 60,000 miles vs. the claimed warranty of 10 years. A wrecked Tesla with a damaged battery pack becomes a total loss in situations where a gas car would be economically repairable. Diagnostic codes are opaque—only Tesla can read them—and parts like battery modules cost 10,000-20,000 USD each. Traditional body shops can't repair them. The supply chain is thin: only a handful of certified repair facilities exist in most regions. This made EV claims unpredictable, which made pricing impossible.

By Q1 2026, major insurers responded by launching dedicated EV commercial auto products with telematics-based pricing. GEICO and others rolled out usage-based models that track driving patterns, braking, acceleration, and real-time battery health. Louisiana regulators began requiring insurers to actuarially justify these dashcam discount programs—one of the first regulatory signals that AI-powered pricing could become standard. Simultaneously, the passenger auto insurance market shifted: telematics adoption reached 68% of US policies by 2025, enabling AI models to reduce claims by 24% through smarter underwriting. The industry achieved a 95.3 combined ratio in 2025—its best result since the pandemic—but that window is narrowing. Rate growth slowed from 15-16% annually (2023-2024) to 7-10% in 2024-2025, and several major carriers filed for rate cuts in California, Florida, and Louisiana by early 2026. Progressive's monthly premiums finally exceeded State Farm's in March 2026 for the first time in 84 years, a shift driven entirely by algorithmic pricing and online distribution. The consolidation pressure is real: insurance agency M&A deals fell 12% year-over-year in 2025, hitting the lowest quarterly total since 2016.

The warranty market got crushed. EV batteries create a new liability type: degenerative failure. A lithium pack loses 2-3% of capacity each year; at year eight, you're at 80% range. Is that still "covered"? Extended warranty providers had already been hobbled by aging vehicle fleets—used cars now outnumber new-car warranty sales at 3.2:1 (2025)—and the FTC was pursuing fraud charges (CarShield settled for 10 million USD in July 2024; Endurance Warranty was sued in March 2025). With EVs creating new, harder-to-model risks, the warranty industry froze. Assurant, the market leader, pivoted: it launched Vehicle Care Technology Plus in March 2025 to bundle car service with smartphone repair. The number of warranty firms grew 0.1% annually from 2020-2025—effectively flat—signaling consolidation without growth. Battery packs under warranty became the focal point: who replaces a 12,000 USD battery at year six if the car is worth 18,000 USD? No one wants to answer that question, so insurers and makers are writing warranties that kick the problem downstream to the used-car market.

Auto insurance (passenger): 95.3 combined ratio in 2025; telematics adoption at 68% of US policies; AI models reduced claims by 24%; Progressive surpassed State Farm in March 2026 for first time in 84 years.

win: Carriers with AI and telematics capabilities win. Progressive's algorithmic pricing machine beat State Farm for the first time in nearly a century because it can price individual risk faster and more accurately. GEICO and other tech-forward insurers launch dedicated EV products that capture the margin opportunity before competitors catch up. Assurant, the warranty leader, diversifies into bundled services (car + phone repair) to escape the commoditized warranty trap. Repair networks that can read EV diagnostics and stock battery modules become gatekeepers; they can charge premiums because they're the only option.
lose: Regional and independent agents get squeezed as M&A deals hit 13-year lows and digital channels (34.7% of warranty sales) bypass dealerships. Traditional body shops that can't repair EVs become obsolete. Smaller warranty providers face a 0.1% annual growth rate—essentially flat—while litigation costs and FTC enforcement drain margins; the trust-damaged warranty segment can't raise prices without losing customers. Customers with older vehicles face spiraling premiums as used-car warranty demand (3.2:1 ratio vs. new) collides with aging EV batteries that nobody knows how to price. State Farm, the 84-year market leader, loses momentum as algorithmic competitors steal monthly premium share.
worry: The biggest risk is that EV repair costs and battery failures will shatter the insurance industry's 2025 recovery before it even took hold. Battery degradation data doesn't exist yet—manufacturers are still hiding warranties in fine print—and the first wave of five-year-old EVs hitting the used market will reveal replacement costs that make cars uninsurable or total-loss-prone. If that data shock hits in 2027-2028, carriers will be forced into another round of double-digit rate hikes just as regulatory pressure builds to freeze rates. The industry could splinter: tech-forward carriers escape with profits while traditional insurers face another cycle of losses.
